implication: committed walk not beaten by parallel scoring in swept range
caveat: coarse grid, single subsample draw per m, one sealed P. Establishes an UPPER bound on the parallel decoder's cost, hence a bound on how much the margin shrinks — not a precise replacement number.
context: raised against Whisper's n=10 hybrid proposal general#2357 rationale (3): 'noiseless simulated C1 = strongest possible classical competitor' holds only WITHIN the frozen algorithm.

llr_extrapolation.reading: The parallel decoder is WORSE, not better. Mechanism: the sealed P has weight 7, so it is covered by only 3^(n-w)=3 of the 6561 emitted bases — uniform sampling spends ~99.95% of copies on bases that cannot see it. The committed sequential walk implicitly CONCENTRATES measurement on bases covering the candidate under test, which is a real (if unremarked) adaptive advantage. My 'linear search is obviously weak' intuition was wrong.

verdict_on_the_challenge: RAISED, TESTED, REFUTED. The published C1 cost survives the most obvious stronger-classical alternative. This is ONE alternative, not a proof of optimality — best-known-classical remains open, and a genuinely adaptive basis-selection strategy is untested.
implementation_warning: FIRST implementation scored candidates by RAW RATE and produced the SAME (flattering) negative conclusion for an entirely WRONG reason — unequal covered-row counts across weights (m/3^w) meant a spurious 1.0 from 3 rows outranked a real 0.97 from 3000. Right answer, wrong reason. Rescored by LLR. A flattering conclusion earned the extra check.
